newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - Adcock looks to merger for growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Adcock looks to merger for growth.

text.p: South African drugs group Adcock Ingram Ltd will look to its recent merger with former rival Premier Pharmaceuticals to secure meaningful growth when it reports year results on Monday, analysts said on Wednesday.
Last month the two firms announced they had now formally merged, but the merger was effective May 1.
Analysts said profits from Premier and the start of cost-savings would see modest profit growth at the group and help offset tight market conditions in the South African pharmaceuticals industry.
"The new company will be a completely different animal from the old Adcock," Frankel Pollack analyst Mark Rule said.

Analysts were predicting earnings per share of 100-112 cents, up from 96 last time, and a dividend of 38-42 cents, up from 36 cents. The consensus figures were for earnings per share of 104.5 cents and a dividend of 39.75 cents.
The merger of the two firms, joining a trend that has gripped the global drugs industry for several years, should reap a host of cost-savings by stripping out duplicated operations.
Adcock already plans to shut its Durban-based self-medication factory and the new group will have one united head office and research and development facility.
Analysts said Adcock should detail more savings from the proposed merger with its results. They are hoping for some indication of their exact size and how many jobs will be shed.
But analysts warned South African drug firms are operating in difficult markets.
Analysts said that, despite an unusually cold winter, fewer South Africans had suffered from illnesses and so cut profits in Adcock's second half.
"By some coincidence people just weren't as sick this year as they were in previous years," one said.
This one-off hit will accentuate the suffering of an industry whose margins are already under pressure from international competitors whose production costs are lower.
As a result some analysts are bearish about South Africa's whole drug manufacturing sector.
"Pharmaceutical companies are not going to get away with the margins they have been doing. I don't want to be in pharmaceutical manufacturing (stocks) at all," one analyst said.
